Normal stress falls automatically on the final syllable of each word. e.g. ['bõ] 'good' [bõ-'bõ] 'confectionery' [ku-'mã ... new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is automatic (non-contrastive) and falls on the final syllable of every word; in connected speech each word keeps its final-syllable stress. A second, emphatic stress type exists (marked with a separate symbol, p. 16), which can shift prominence, e.g. /lavi u/ 'your life' realised [laviju] with stress on final /i/ or [laviu] with stress on the pronoun /u/ (p. 36).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in the snippets seen; the double-quote mark in the p. 45 example ("katsi'le, "kuma'se) appears to be the emphatic-stress symbol defined on p. 16, not secondary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Emphatic stress (type b, p. 44-45) can fall elsewhere than the final syllable; the p. 45 snippet reads that in that context 'normal stress is retained on the final syllable' but the preceding clause is cut off in the snippet. Elision/glide phenomena at word junctures interact with stress placement (p. 36).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level ('final syllable of each word'), with a note that this holds in connected speech (phrase example on p. 45). The 1984 book is the 1967 UWI dissertation (fieldwork 1964-67, Castries area), structuralist description. Quote assembled from Google Books partial-view snippets (pp. 44, 45); the full section was not readable, so the ellipses mark snippet cut-offs, not editorial omissions.
new_statements.identity_note: Carrington's data are the St. Lucia variety (fieldwork 1964-67, Castries area; dialect variation explicitly not analysed), i.e. sain1246 proper. Glottolog also files Dominica (Taylor, Amastae), Grenada (Phillip) and Trinidad (Thomas 1869, Lugo 2017) French Creole under sain1246; the Thomas 1869 final-stress remark examined here is for the Trinidad variety and is only corroborative.
